title: Eighth commandment (CCC 2464–2499)
hookLine: truth, reputation and not spreading faults

cards: "Did you hear about Dan?" Five words, and the room leans in. What comes next might even be true.
Dan did lose his temper at the meeting. Dan's marriage is in trouble. Nobody is lying.
And yet, by the end of lunch, a whole table of people who will never help Dan think a little less of him, and Dan doesn't know it happened. The Catechism has a name for that, and it isn't lying.

teach.b: The commandment, from Exodus in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour." A courtroom picture: someone lies, and an innocent person pays.

The Catechism calls truthfulness the virtue of being true in deed and word, and of guarding against two-facedness. Then it widens the frame, uncomfortably. It names three sins against a person's reputation.
Rash judgment: assuming the worst about someone without enough to go on. Calumny: saying false things that damage them.
And detraction: telling someone's real faults to people who didn't know them, without a serious reason. Real faults. Dan really did lose his temper.
It still counts as a wrong, because a good name belongs to a person, and you can take it from them with the truth.

The Catechism offers a habit for the other side, quoting Ignatius of Loyola: be readier to give a good reading to what a neighbor says than to condemn it, and if the words seem wrong, ask what was meant.

When harm is done, it has to be repaired, even if the one who caused it has been forgiven. That can be hard: walking back into the lunchroom to say, I shouldn't have said that about Dan. One more thing.

Not everyone has a right to every truth. Some things are kept for love's sake, or for safety, or under a seal, like the confessional. Truth, in this commandment, is not a weapon for whoever wants one.

how: Catholics examine themselves on the eighth commandment before confession, asking about lies, rash judgment, calumny and detraction; the Church teaches that harm done to a reputation should be repaired where possible.

games.q: at lunch, a coworker says, "did you hear about Dan?" what you know is true, and nobody else at the table knows it. what does the Catechism call passing it on without a serious reason?
games.why: detraction: revealing another's real faults to people who didn't know them. calumny is when the thing said is false.

practice: Bring to mind something you know about someone, true or half true, that you've been tempted to pass on, and without replaying the details, just hold the person's name.
Picture them walking into the room, then picture the story set down, staying with you. If you pray, ask God to guard their good name; if not, let the story end with you.

wordCard.voice: The eighth commandment. You shall not bear false witness: in Catholic teaching, a call to live in the truth, and to guard every neighbor's good name, even from true things told without need. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a false witness — the phrase in the commandment, Exodus 20:16.

carryVoice: Your line: guard reputations. A good name belongs to the one who carries it. Go gently.
